title: Effect of changing data, and comparing centers across sets
subtitle: One-variable data: Distributions and measures of center and spread · 19 official questions

sections.heading: Where this sits for you
body: **19 of the official questions in One-variable data: Distributions and measures of center and spread are this one** — 4 Easy, 3 Medium, 12 Hard.
It is top-heavy: most versions are Hard, so it only earns study time once your target actually requires that tier.

sections.heading: How to spot it
body: You are looking at this pattern when:
- The question asks what happens to the mean and/or median when a value is added (often an outlier), or which statement 'must be true' about two sets' means or medians.
- You may get box plots, frequency tables with symbolic values, or several tables to rank by mean.
- Roman-numeral I/II answer formats are common.

sections.heading: The method
body: - 1) Adding an extreme value pulls the mean hard toward it but moves the median at most one position, so check whether the middle value actually changes.
- 2) Box plots show medians only, never means, so any mean claim is not 'must be true'.
- 3) For symmetric tables, the mean is the center of symmetry, so find the one that isn't symmetric and see which way it leans.

sections.heading: Where Desmos fits
body: Usually null: these are reasoning questions about how measures behave, often with symbolic or unspecified values.
For numeric frequency tables you can check means with mean(values, frequencies).

sections.heading: What it is built to catch
body: You assume the median shifts as much as the mean when an outlier is added, or that it always changes.
Or you infer something about the mean from a box plot.
Or, with 'must be true' wording, you pick a claim that is merely possible.

sections.heading: You are losing these
body: Before you choose, say out loud what the question is asking for — not what you solved for.
You assume the median shifts as much as the mean when an outlier is added, or that it always changes.
